comments.text:
or 3060? 60 meaning 6gb ?? And 3080 80 for the 8Gb model . And yes the X meaning the more advance GPU in that series in this case 3000 series cards.

I never go by names or models any ways . I Go by Core Clock and Memory clock . I see this all the time Same Model but the Core clocks are different and the memory speed.  The Size of the memory isn't important Unless your Playing on a 50" screen TV at 4k  .  simple more pixel resolution requires more memory .

Learn This back in the Day with 640 x 480
Pixels: 640 x 480 = 307,200 pixels
Color Depth: 24 bits per pixel (3 bytes)
Total Memory: 307,200 pixels * 3 bytes/pixel = 921,600 bytes
In Kilobytes: 921,600 bytes / 1024 bytes/KB ≈ 900 KB . 
3D  at 640 x40 accelerated 1.2 mb (But then you need Resolution texture memory so it would be Doubled. But 2.4 Never became a standard .  From the Old Voodoo 1 algorithm  2 meg 3D  accelerated 2meg Textura memory = 4 mb.
 Voodoo 2 800 x 600 8mb total .  4 meg 3D  accelerated 4meg Textura memory = 8 mb.
4k 8gb  3D  accelerated +  8gb Textura memory = 16gb total . That Playing on screen that is big enough to take advantage of  4k . Your 24" Monitor doesn't really do that . 
And VRAM is also Superior to your Motherboard Ram . VRAM "no wait states" . VS Standard DDR at any Speed depends on Manufacture but can have wait states up 24ns. some lower Like Corsair is 17ns  Older EDO was 50-90ns. But the GPU can add latency.  

You Don't need 8gb to run on a 17" Monitor playing at 720 p .  Or  12gb on a 22" Monitor playing at 1080p . When 6gb will work just fine . What's more Import is the Core Clock( reduces studdinging or elemites it also affects  the memory Speed .  Not All GDDR is created equal . 
So don't ever believe the Marketing hype . Stop being programmed by the TV commercial ot the reddit post.  And Read the white papers for yourself.

It may not be the card for the mass, but perfectly suits my need

comments.text:
Ha Linus, I got bamboozled by NVidia before you did!

When my NVidia Riva TNT2 in my PC died (paired with a Katmai Pentium III at 500Mhz), I asked my dad to buy a new GPU - a TNT2 Ultra or even GeForce if possible.

What did he came home with? A TNT M64, which could barely keen up with the original TNT from 2 years prior. What is the TNT2 M64, younger viewers might ask? It's a normal TNT2... but with it's bandwidth cut in half from 2.4 GB/s down to 1.2GB/s. Now just try and imagine such a steep cut on a modern GPU.

Even worse, we went from 32 Megabyte VRAM down to 16 Megabyte - and we were lucky we didn't get the 8 Megabyte version of the M64. And had he paid the equivalent of $15 more, we would have ended up with a TNT2 Pro... which was easily twice as fast as the M64 in many games.

comments.text:
The GT 730. There was a DDR4 and DDR3 (iirc, I know for sure it was a RAM architecture difference) variant, costing around $60 and $30 USD respectively. I found this out while helping a really poor guy from India on the old TomsHardware forums.

He basically scrounged up an old PC and wanted to play some older 2D games his friend was playing with their own 730. He said he saved up for 3 months to pay the ruple equivalent of $30 USD (it was something like 4200-4800 at the time).

But his couldn't play one of the games in question. I don't quite remember what we checked first—some easy hardware things, I think—but he gave me the link to the Indian Amazon page he bought the card on and after some thorough examination of the details, discovered what Nvidia had done.

It felt awful to inform him he bought the wrong card and that the card he wanted and needed was double the price.

This was before the 1030 GDDR5 switched to DDR4 scandal, so when that happened my thoughts were "so they did it again".

I don't know if that's because they're evil, they don't want to redesign and pay for new packaging all the time (which can cost quite a bit), or there's that much miscommunication... maybe it's a little bit of all of the above.

Regardless, I really wish honesty would take precedence over whatever they're smoking.

Just make a generic green box with "Nvidia" and a space for stamped specifications instead of cool "3049Ti" logos for each variant.

comments.text:
As if it wasn't already confusing before, this absolutely sucks. 

I worked at a semiconductor manufacturing plant before. I can understand why they segment and salvage some dies as it makes sense to be economical and make use of something that can still work but for lower tier products if they underperform functional and parametric tests (which may or may not indicate physical die issues).

Think of the i3, i5, i7, and i9 Intel chips as an example (not my IRL job, only for analogy's sake). The dies would be the same structurally. However, along the long manufacturing process, some of the dies would fail i9 and i7 tests but pass i5 and i3 standards. They would be "binned" or sorted accordingly. Sometimes, we even had to purposefully sort i5 chips into i3 if there was more demand for it just to fulfill orders. There were some chips that were only renames with additional tests too but basically the same structurally. The opposite happens too where the same chip is tested with less or looser coverage and that is sold as a different product altogether.

Naturally, if the yield of higher end dies are lower, they would struggle to keep up with demand. From NVIDIA's side, it seems they have a tougher time sorting the products into their existing product categories whereby the supposedly 3080 chip does not quite meet the standards of its target yet is a bit above a 3050 but less than 3060. Knowing the price difference is larger if they tag it at 3050, they're just likely minimizing loss or maximizing and salvaging whatever profit they could gain. Thus, they end up creating a weaker 3060 variant overall.

Long story short, this is not new to semiconductor manufacturing. It's just that these modern processing units are so complex and expensive to build that I get it why they want to salvage whatever they can. On the part of the consumers, however, it really is a pain if companies can't make it easier to manage expectations on performance and price associated with a product name or product tiers.

comments.text:
What makes a high-end GPU is the die size, as that is the limiting factor for GPUs. A high-end GPU is a die size 80-95% the Reticle Limit, a.k.a the maximum size a single chip can be on the current process node without additional tech. 
The RTX 4090 is indeed a high-end GPU, but that's where it ends, the rest of this generation is named a higher tier and priced at a higher tier than what they are selling you.

The rtx 4080(Super) is a 70 class GPU, it has a die size of 379mm^2, the rtx 3070 has a die size of 392mm^2.
The rtx 4070Ti is a 60 class GPU, as it has a 294mm^2 die size and the rtx 3060 has a die size of 276mm^2
The rtx 4070 is a 50Ti class GPU, as it is a cut down RTX 4070Ti.
The rtx 4060Ti is a 50 class GPU at 188mm^2 die size, the rtx 3050 8GB has a die size of 226mm^2 cut from the 276mm^2 of the RTX 3060
The rtx 4060 is a 30/40 class GPU at 147mm^2 die size.

The reticle limit is 851mm^2, so a high-end GPU should be 650-750mm^2 like the rtx 2080Ti which is infact a 754mm^2 die size.
A mid range Chip, regardless if it's a GPU, CPU, Micro Controller, etc, is a chip that is around half the reticle size, so about 400-450mm^2 die size. 

The only other 2 generations where Nvidia screwed with the naming and prices are the gtx 1000 series, where the gtx 1080 is a 314mm^2 die size chip, thus the gtx 1080 is a 60 class card. The other generation was the gtx 600 series where again the gtx 680 was a 60 class chip at 298mm^2 die size(keep in mind the reticle limit was lower for 28nm) and they even had it called a gtx 660 a few months before release. It was also the first Gx104 chip to be called a gtx 80 class card, before that they were all Gx100/200.

Nvidia's Deceptive GPU Naming Scheme: Confusing Consumers for Profit

* 0:00: Nvidia is re-releasing less powerful GPUs with the same name as older, more powerful ones, misleading consumers. Examples include:
    * 1:46: The RTX 3050 6GB performs significantly worse than the original 3050 8GB.
    * 5:09: The RTX 3060 8GB has a reduced memory bus compared to the original 3060 12GB, leading to lower performance.
* 6:14: This practice of misleading naming schemes isn't new and has been seen with older GPUs like the GTX 660 and GeForce 4 MX.
* 3:02: Budget GPU shoppers are often less informed and more vulnerable to this deceptive naming scheme, relying on name recognition over in-depth research.
* 9:03: While Nvidia sometimes has legitimate reasons for releasing different versions of GPUs (like salvaging faulty dies), their lack of clear labeling and communication is a major problem.
* 6:14:  The video argues that as the market leader, Nvidia has a responsibility to be more transparent and set a better example for the industry.
* 10:10: The ultimate conclusion is that Nvidia's GPU naming scheme is confusing and often misleading, prioritizing profit over consumer clarity. The name no longer reliably indicates performance, leaving consumers to do extensive research to avoid being tricked.

comments.text:
Oh the joy of building a new PC every couple of years... And honestly, I am a bit past the age when it seemed so important to keep constant track of tech releases. I might still watch some videos, but find my self actually ignoring most of the stuff. In the end most of it is quite irrelevant to me anyhow.

But then when I start thinking about a new build... Usually start with a CPU, then match it with a MB that hopefully actually supports it... At one point there actually was this sort of thing where they would say on product information "supported", but when you actually built your system, it would be like CPU error, and then when you go back and ask they reply something like "oh yea, it is kind of supported, you just need a BIOS upgrade to get it working... And back then bios upgrades didn't work without a CPU that is actually supported and succes of the upgrade was a bit of hit and miss game. Since then things have improved as one can upgrade BIOS without CPU and they usually work without any incidents... 

Anyhow... once past all the CPU/MB pain... Maybe I should quickly mention cooling, as I had once issues with, once again product information declaring "AM5 support" (or was it 4, well whatever), and then going like "oh yea, but you need to get this optional mounting hardware (wich was being sold by no-one)... So in the end I had bought like a new water block that was not any better than the one I allready had, and was basically forced to do a DIY hackjob to somehow actually mount it. 

But moving on to GPU's, it is a literal mountain of work trying to decipher wich is outdated overpriced junk and wich is mid tier good value for the price GPU... And as a little note, I usually go for low or mid tier GPU's as most my builds are essentially for just general office use, so often gaming is something I can ignore completely. And for multi-role computers mid-tier GPU is usually fine enough, they usually do just fine on most games and don't need crazy amounts of power, wich would likely lead to noisy cooling solutions, wich is not-cool for living room entertainment solutions. Anyway, to further complicate matters then there are even availability worries. Recently I waited for literal months for components, after wich the parts supplier declared unable to deliver due to lack of requested GPU, wich was supposed to be "in stock", or "coming soon"... So I had to redo much of the research to find another one, dodging atleast a half a dozen with uncertain availability. In the end I think I might have gotten a better deal than the one I chose originally... But I really wish it had not been so much work.

And now you are telling me, that on top of everything else allready making PC building a bit of a pain, the GPU makers are actively trying to deceive and scam people... Even if not allways entirely intentionally, but creating these more or less shady naming schemes that are definately not ideal for the sake of clarity.

And after a long'ish rant on what is annoying about PC building... Please don't come telling me "why build if it is that bad". Yes, I know I could just pick my price range and buy prebuilt. But I actually do like building PC's, there are just a few things that could be made a little bit easier.

comments.text:
Its not just the Nforce chipset with an IGP but all the AGP and PCI addoncards in the GeForce 4 MX line are just die shrunk GeForce 2 MX chips with a video decoder added and DDR ram as standard.
Even worse is the "Walmart" GeForce 4 MX cards with its 64bit or sometimes 32bit bus instead of the full 128bit.
And it gets worse, the GeForce 4 MX 440 should have had 500Mhz DDR, most decent cards have 400Mhz but some have even slower.
I have one with 286Mhz ram in a 64bit configuration, on top of that they underclocked the ram to 266Mhz.
So in the end the bandwidth is on par with the slowest GeForce 2  MX 200 64bit bus version, not the GeForce 2 MX 400 128bit bus version everyone bought back in 2001.

The problem with the GeFroce4 MX is that it cant run anything that requires a GeForce3 minimum and even if you can run games that support programmable shaders you can get a hard performance hit, Halo suffers a lot on te GF2 or GF4 MX line relative to the GeForce 3 or a proper GeForce 4.

But if you know what your buying a proper Geforce4 MX 440 with 500Mhz DDR at 128bit or the less common MX 460 with 550Mhz DDR they are decently fast, the GPU is clocked high so if you did not play cutting edge games they where fine budget cards.

But for every Good GF4 MX out there there are a bunch of Walmart editions....

Honestly a lot of this seems both on Nvidia, but also the board partners, especially before the Pascal generation. The board partners at that time were able to offer more designs that were far from reference. That's also the issue with the laptop chips. You have issues with them not disclosing wattage, but the Laptop manufacturers are the ones that decide TDP there.

Think there's a big market segment which these naming practices harm which didn't get enough detail... Prebuilt PC's

Prebuilt consumers often see these GPUs as part of a complete system, and can 'score' a small discount on the same specs for 'a little less v-ram'. These are often the most poorly informed consumers, and get caught out by unforeseen bottlenecks when their PC arrives. They trust builders to choose good components, and builders almost ALWAYS cut costs with these lower-end but similarly named GPUs at the expense of the uninformed consumer.

Personally got bamboozled by my first introduction to PC gaming with a 1060 3GB vs 6GB, and can 100% see how these practices help to drive bottom line for Nvidia and retailers alike.

comments.text:
The worst AMD has done with graphics card naming, that I can recall off hand, is the RX 580 2048SP.  Same amount of memory as the RX 580, but a lower shader count.  But the shader count is part of the name, so the only chance of someone getting confused is if they truncate the full name and assume that "RX 580 2048SP" is somehow the same as "RX 580".  Less likely than if the only difference is the VRAM size.

I was about to comment about the GeForce 4 MX fiasco, but I see the video has already brought it up.  By far the worst instance of deceptive naming.  It actually held back gaming for a period of time, because it's relatively low price made people buy it in droves, meaning developers had to limit the functionality of their games to allow them to run on that decrepit hardware.

Edit:  Adding this for context, for those who end up reading this but don't know why the GeForce 4 MX was such a fiasco.  This was very early days in 3D graphics, and the functionality difference between GeForce 2 and GeForce 4 was immense.  Any game developer who wanted to make sure their game ran on the despicably popular GeForce 4 MX would have to eschew many advances in 3D rendering, because they simply weren't supported on the MX card (i.e. a GeForce 2 card with a different name).  ATI never did anything like that.  Neither has AMD, though by 2006, when AMD bought ATI, the opportunity to do such a thing was pretty much gone.  In a more modern (though still quite aged) context, the equivalent would be releasing a card capable of only DX8 with naming shared by cards supporting DX12.

comments.text:
Why skip arguably the most egregious example? The Geforce 8 8800 series.
The GS and GT both came with G92 cores by default, the GS being hamstrung by a 192-bit bus, with the GT having a 256-bit bus.
The GTS, GTX, and Ultra came with G80 cores by default, having either a 320-bit bus on the GTS or a 384-bit bus on the GTX and Ultra.
And then they introduced the GTS G80-112 followed by the GTS G92.

This resulted in a situation where the only reason why the Ultra and GTX were still the fastest cards in practice was their memory bus bandwidth. As the G92 core was significantly faster than the G80. The 8800GTS G92 pushed 30% more GFLOPS than the 8800 Ultra. Same with the GS pushing more GFLOPS than the GTS G80 versions.

So if you're asking the question "which Geforce 8 8800 is the fastest" the answer is really up for debate. 
The GS was faster than a GTS G80 in GFLOPS, but not in FPS due to the massive bandwidth difference. However a GTS G80-112 was faster than a GS even in GFLOPS. Now a GT was faster than a GTS G80, for most things, unless memory bandwidth was a consideration. It could push about as many GFLOPS as a GTX, but again the GTX and Ultra had much wider memory buses at 384-bit versus 256-bit on the GT.
And yet a GTS G92 was the fastest in GFLOPS, but lagged behind the Ultra only because of it's hamstrung 256-bit bus and only 512MB of VRAM, even though the GT did have a 1GB option, but still at the same 256-bit bus. So VRAM performance was quite a bit slower than the 768MB a GTX or Ultra had on it's 384-bit bus.

It was a mess. And on the box all they advertised was Geforce 8 8800 GTS or GT. Good luck figuring out which one best suits your needs.

It could be argued that at least they were labeled differently, baring the MX suffix but they were not even related to GF4 TI cards, hell, they weren't even related to GF3. Nvidia love messing with people's heads with their naming. It will never stop unless the global bodies in charge of setting marketing restrictions make it illegal to do so.

Creating a Youtube video acussing successful tech giants like Nvidia and AMD of corporate greed sounds a tad like hype to me. comments.text:
The Titan X situation was so much worse. It's actually a russian doll case of misleading marketing. Nvidia initially released the Titan X, which was a Maxwell card comprised of the full fat GM102 die and 12GB of RAM, basically a GTX 980ti with double the memory and a 10~15% performance boost. Then they released the Titan X. Literally the exact same name, but this time a card comprised of an almost full fat GP102 die and 12GB of RAM, basically a GTX 1080ti with a slight performance boost and an extra 1GB of RAM. This REALLY annoyed the community, so they called it the Titan Xp since the two cards were in completely different performance classes, like the pascal version was very nearly twice as fast in some case. THEN Nvidia released an ACTUAL Titan Xp, which WAS the full fat GP102 die with slightly faster 12GB of RAM, giving about a 10% improvement over the last card, but the name basically made it impossible to call it anything that wouldn't confuse anyone. Call it the Titan Xp and you're going to confuse people in reviews because that's what people were already calling the last card in reviews, but it's not what you see on the shelf. Call it the Titan Xpp so that people don't get confused by reviews and you confuse them when they get to the shelf. In retrospect, people now call them Titan X Maxwell, Titan X Pascal, and Titan Xp, but the damage has already been done. Tinfoil hat, I think they did it on purpose to implicitly tell reviewers to never make up names for their products.
When I walked into Microcenter during the fiasco, I saw so many open box titan cards, especially the Maxwell ones. The thing that shocked me the most was that Nvidia ever dared to screw with their enthusiast buyers, but I probably should've taken it as a hint that their enthusiast buyers were now in the enterprise space and we didn't matter anymore to them.

Agree on part of incorrect labeling but memory bus lengths has to correlate with how they are connected with adress bus. They simply cannot have memory banks attached in series like CPUs but have different architecture to have that extra bandwidth andnit comes with extra lanes.

Just a tradeoff between different memory architectures and how memory controllers work. The labeling are supposed to be on par with performance but that's not the case as GPUs and softwares that use them have wide variety of combinations.

comments.text: One more note on the naming convention, the released and sample specs are for reference designs. Nvidia in the consumer market do not directly sell cards with own branding, but they are bundled with 3rd party manufacturers, which take in core chip and then assemble the whole PCI card. The same is true for AMD, and there are many cases where naming is just not right.  May be it's the core reason why cards get misleading names, but sure, they should be able to control on what chips and configs make a certain trade name and a fixed SKU.  There's no industry standard when it comes to companies implementing different versions of the same chip and market it. OEM and enterprise cards will have different specs esp in quadro and radeon pro will always have different specs depending on who is making them and who they are selling to. Some customers actually benefit from domain specific SKUs and its usually profitable as well.

comments.text: When nvidia creates a model slot, it's not out of a goodness of their heart, but to create a price point and plug a hole in the model grid and the market where the competitor (singular) might run away with their customers if they didn't do that. Then there's a question of how much you can cut down an existing semiconductor or whether you spin up a new one, which might be uneconomical. Sometimes things align just right that they sort of overdeliver. Where the next step down on clock or compute would look too suspicious or where the next cut down on memory bus would lead to bad consequences, so they end up releasing something actually nice. Sometimes it's due to misprediction of what the competitor might counter with.

That's been the norm in the semiconductor industry for quite a while now. The chips that can't pass at full power get binned down to something a bit slower and sold anyways. They typically function just fine at the lower speed, but have stability issues if all the hardware is unlocked or if overclocked.

Ultimately, it's a good thing as the alternative is to either throw out those chips or kill the warranty to keep the company solvent.

comments.text: @ShiroKage009   I had been using a 970 till it suffered a fatal accident a year ago and i vehemently disagree. 9 years of use. For the price point, it turned out to be a super resilient and well performing card. The slow half-gigabyte is transparent to software except headless CUDA compute workloads. Realistically you need 300MB for DWM (desktop window manager) so you weren't missing more than about 200MB of fast memory vs. a 4GB card. None of the DX12/Vulkan games which need 4GB VRAM stumbled on the card due to VRAM scarcity, though some stumble on 900 series in general due to architectural deficiencies. In an actual videogame, you simply have gigabytes of VRAM that are "cold" and are occupied in the expectation that the data loaded there is needed soon, but you literally can't plaster more than a couple gigabytes of data into one frame, you plain don't have the throughput to make it happen, and the drivers appear to do pretty well with using the slow and fast VRAM appropriately.

comments.text:
It reminds me of the conundrum  a company faces when their partner manufacturer ships them an order that had sub-par components substituted, throwing the product out of spec.

Imagine a small company who’s whole production run and cash flow is dependent on the sale of these good that are now varying from what they advertised or sent in review samples.

Naturally the appropriate response is to own up and be honest with the buyers, but it does present a moral dilemma, especially if the issue is so egregious as to make the whole shipment undesirable and unsellable. 

If it’s really bad quality, it’s even more reason not to burn your customer, but also even more incentive to sweep it under the rug.  

Sure everyone wants to do good and feel like they always were the good guy who made the right choice, but such is the nature of moral dilemmas that they are challenging to ones ethics, it may be that the company will go defunct if they don’t move the product at the full price.  George and his family and little Timmie’s Christmas all ride on George being employed not only this year but next year too. 

This cascade of rip offs may going all the way up the supply chain, where at each point the low quality stuff was sold to the next guy who made a product with it to then be in someone else’s product.  

Which is why ethics in mining is perhaps the most important. If we can pre-empt that chain reaction at the foundation species of the supply chain. Perhaps it would make the whole world more ethical as a result of dodging those tough moral dilemmas. 

Perhaps a type of insurance or government assistance for when a company gets burned by a supplies could also be an effective measure to break the chains of forwarded issues.  Or just access to capital to take a loan to absorb the loss, so a company can roll with the punches instead of being forced into that tight decision to either be honest or go under. 

I know product revisions (1.1-1.2) often reflect a change in parts available from suppliers. But this behavior from Nvidia is the opposite of that, a revision with the same product label.  Clearly they have no moral dilemma forced by the threat of survival. But I wonder if their supply chain has any role in what we see here, perhaps a reflection of their attitudes towards their partners.

comments.text:
@BestGirlsBiggestFan   Most of the connectors were defined in optional supplementary notices since they were not necessary for device to implement the corresponding USB standard, which is primarily electrical and logical. Also in supplementary notices were other optional features like OTG, Charging and (vehicle) Accessory. On USB major versions 2 and 3, signalling was overhauled with new modes being introduced (HighSpeed and SuperSpeed respectively) and new Classes being defined. Before version 4, the versioning made decent sense, but since then, good bloody luck.

Many of the supplementary notices barely exist on paper and weren't relevant in physical reality. Like, by the time OTG semiconductors were actually available, this functionality got folded into Micro B connector, early obsoleting miniature A and AB variants.

Also you're forgetting how old USB 2.0 is. The spec was published in 2000. Mini, Micro etc connectors were defined after and against the 2.0 spec.

What i did find iffy for a while were many devices advertising "USB 2.0" and implying speediness while implementing only FullSpeed signalling which was already defined in USB 1.x. But they did have USB 2.0 extended descriptors. So both a lie and a truth. Some USB 2.0 Classes even only foresee FullSpeed signalling to begin with, no HighSpeed support, because that's what made sense.

comments.text:
Budget buyers should be the ones doing the most research. As they often have the most to loose from a bad purchase decision.

Buyers in this segment can fall into many camps, but one of those is people who simply do not have a lot of extra money to burn, and need to get the best bang for what bucks they can spend.

It is an unfortunate fact that companies will prey on the low income population, by fooling them to part money on what looks like a good bargain, but is far from it.

False economy is a thing. Where things like lower quality and higher price per unit comes into play. Ex, you might find a battery two pack for a buck at a dollar store, but those same batteries can be ten for $3 at a regular store. Yes you spend more, but you get much more for your money. It's similar to the bulk buying idea. Sometimes spending more now saves you money in the long run.

Unfortunately many in that situation can't afford to spend the extra.

The high cost of poor living as they say... Interest rates on loans, medical care, and so much more, cost the low income population more than those with better financial means for the same thing.

A bit of a rant on the screwed up nature of our society...

I've been 'burned' by this once before, bought a 710 GT as a simple stopgap card when my old Core 2 Duo system got damaged by lightning, just needed a simple Vulkan capable GPU for cheap.
Well, turns out NVIDIA made two different 710's, one with a 128bit memory bus, the other with 64bit... You'd think the 128bit card would be the (slightly) better card, but no. The 128bit card is Fermi based, the 64bit one is Kepler, and guess what? NVIDIA never supported Vulkan on Fermi, despite the GPU being physically capable.
I wasn't happy, but it wasn't a huge deal, because a few weeks later AIB RX 480 cards came out and I picked up one of those and that was my GPU for a very long time. lol

comments.text:
What Linus is saying about upgrading a Dell Optiplex is actually Pretty on Point.

I recently came across a Dell Optiplex 7060 in a dumpster (yeah, you read that right!). Normally, I'd just walk on by, but something caught my eye—this thing still had 16GB of RAM and an Intel i7-8700 CPU. I knew I had to take it home and see if I could bring it back to life.

Once I got it home, I went to work cleaning it up. I removed the old cooler, cleaned off the crusty thermal paste, and replaced it with some fresh Grizzly Bear thermal paste. I then went to town on all the dust that had accumulated over the years. After a thorough cleaning, I decided to see how much potential this machine really had.

First, I upgraded the graphics by installing an MSI GeForce RTX 3050 6GB Low Profile GPU. This was the perfect fit for the compact case. Then, I doubled the RAM by adding two additional 8GB sticks, bringing the total to a hefty 32GB.



In-Depth Analysis of Benchmarks for Upgraded Dell Optiplex 7060
After finding and upgrading the Dell Optiplex 7060 I found in a dumpster, I was eager to see how it would perform, especially after adding the MSI GeForce RTX 3050 6GB Low Profile GPU and bumping the RAM to 32GB. Here’s a deeper dive into the benchmarks I ran and what they reveal about the system's performance.

1. UserBenchmark Overview
UserBenchmark Results:

UserBenchmark provides a great snapshot of overall system performance. Here’s what stood out:

Gaming: The GPU scored a 68.6% in the Gaming category, indicating it’s well-suited for 1080p gaming, with some capability to handle 1440p gaming depending on the title and settings.
Desktop: The desktop score was very high (93%), which is expected given the i7-8700 CPU and the increased 32GB RAM. This means it’s more than capable of handling multitasking, productivity tasks, and moderate gaming without breaking a sweat.
Workstation: Scoring 54.1% in this category suggests the system is decent for some workstation tasks, like video editing or 3D rendering, but it won’t rival high-end workstations. This is likely due to the limitations of the RTX 3050 in more demanding professional workloads.
Overall, these results indicate a balanced machine that can handle a range of tasks, from gaming to productivity, though it won't excel at the most demanding professional applications.

2. 3DMark Benchmarks
Steel Nomad Light:

In the Steel Nomad Light benchmark, the system hit the highest score ever recorded for its configuration. This benchmark primarily tests the GPU’s capability in handling lighter gaming loads and 3D rendering tasks.

Graphics Score: The RTX 3050 did an excellent job here, indicating it can handle most games at medium to high settings at 1080p without any issues. It also suggests that this setup is ideal for esports titles and other less graphically intense games.
Time Spy:

Time Spy is a more demanding DirectX 12 benchmark, and here the system’s performance was solid but showed some limitations.

Graphics Score: The system scored well, but it’s clear that while it can manage 1440p gaming, and even some 4K, pushing 4K at 60fps in the latest AAA titles might be beyond its capabilities. The RTX 3050, while powerful, doesn’t have the muscle to handle the most graphically intense games at the highest resolutions and settings.

CPU Score: The i7-8700 continues to show its strengths in this benchmark, handling the physics and CPU-intensive tasks with ease. This makes the system very capable for multitasking, streaming while gaming, and handling background processes without impacting gaming performance.

Fire Strike:

Fire Strike is another demanding test, but it focuses on DirectX 11. Here’s how the system performed:

Graphics Score: The RTX 3050 delivered good results again, confirming its ability to handle modern games at 1080p and 1440p with settings ranging from medium to high. However, ultra settings, particularly at 1440p or 4K, will push the limits of this card.

Combined Score: The overall performance in this benchmark is balanced, showing that the CPU and GPU are well-matched for mid-range gaming setups. It can handle older AAA titles at high settings and newer ones at medium settings.

Port Royal:

Port Royal is a benchmark designed to test ray tracing performance, which is one of the newer and more demanding graphical features.

Graphics Score: While the RTX 3050 can handle ray tracing, it’s clear that it’s not its strong suit, especially in 4K. For ray tracing at 1080p, you might need to turn down some other settings to maintain a playable frame rate. However, the results were respectable for this class of GPU, making it a viable option for gamers looking to experiment with ray tracing without breaking the bank.
General Performance Observations
1080p Gaming: Across all benchmarks, the system shines at 1080p. You can expect smooth performance in nearly all titles at this resolution, even with settings cranked up.
1440p Gaming: The system is capable of 1440p gaming, though you may need to adjust settings to maintain high frame rates in more demanding games.
4K Gaming: This is where the system starts to struggle, particularly in the latest AAA titles with ray tracing enabled. While it’s possible to game at 4K, it’s more suited for older or less demanding titles, or you’ll need to reduce settings significantly.

Conclusion
The Dell Optiplex 7060, after some TLC and a few key upgrades, has been transformed into a very capable machine. The benchmarks show that it’s well-suited for 1080p and even 1440p gaming, as well as general productivity tasks. While it’s not a high-end gaming rig, it punches above its weight for its components and would make an excellent budget or entry-level gaming PC. It’s also a great example of how older hardware can still be viable with the right upgrades, making this dumpster find a real gem!

@justin_fps  One in the United States would be 15 USC Chapter 2 Subchapter 1 Section 45 (a) (1) "Unfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce, and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, are hereby declared unlawful."

IMHO it is a deceptive practice to use the same product name in this way. If you say RTX 3050 8GB and RTX 3050 6GB, this clearly implies the difference is the suffix. It is arguable however.

Looking at Nvidia's own website doesn't make them look great either. The 30 series simple comparison chart does list the 3050 8 and 6 GB separately. However, there are also TWO 3050 8GB variants. Reading a footnote, the "OEM" 3050 8GB has a lower CUDA core count and boost clock than the one on the chart. They also group both 3080s into the same product column, even though the 10GB model has a lower core count. Compare that to the 3060 column, where both the 12GB and 8GB models supposedly have the same core count. 

And then when you open the detailed specs, it gets even more unintelligible. Like the 3080 Ti that has a lower boost clock than either of the 3080s, the 3080 10GB has a higher base clock than the 12 GB, etc.

Basically, it's clear that the name of the product is neither representing the components in it, nor a performance standard. But yet that is the primary identifier in advertisements and on product packaging. I consider that deceptive.

Yes, I know many other corporations do this too. That doesn't make it right, ethical, or legal.

comments.text:
@Tense  I appreciate your effort. All these views and you're about the only one to even try. But I don't think it says anything specifically relevant to the situation here. Quote:

-----

In determining whether advertising is misleading, account shall be taken of all its features, and in particular of any information it contains concerning:

(a) the characteristics of goods or services, such as their availability, nature, execution, composition, method and date of manufacture or provision, fitness for purpose, uses, quantity, specification, geographical or commercial origin or the results to be expected from their use, or the results and material features of tests or checks carried out on the goods or services;

(b) the price or the manner in which the price is calculated, and the conditions on which the goods are supplied or the services provided;

(c) the nature, attributes and rights of the advertiser, such as his identity and assets, his qualifications and ownership of industrial, commercial or intellectual property rights or his awards and distinctions.


-----

In other words, the rule is that the box must accurately say what's inside. There's no rule that says "the name can't remind you of a different name that's visibly different". Which is precisely the case of the 3050 8gb vs 3050 6gb. What's the claim? "I read the first 4 characters of the title and ignored literally everything else on the box?"

And I'll remind you the long-established precedent of car manufacturing. Cars frequently change from year to year and literally use the same name for decades. Are there a bunch of lawsuits from people who thought the 2018 Mustang GT was the same as the 1982 Mustang GT?

That said, yeah a court could rule whatever they want because when you have nuclear weapons who's gonna stop you? But I'm going to need someone to explain to me how an Accord can have different models but a 3050 can't.

p.s. My "conspiracy" comment was directed at the person who said there was definitely a law but no one will enforce it because bribes. You'll notice they didn't offer up any legal text like you did.
